title: Charlemagne's Capitulare: Magic as Heresy in Carolingian Empire
description: Charlemagne's Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae (785 CE) and related Carolingian capitularies defined magic practices including divination, storm-raising, and sacrifice to demons as capital crimes in the newly conquered Saxon territories. These laws represented the first systematic attempt by a Christian ruler to legislate against magic as a heresy rather than merely a civil disorder, treating magical practitioners as enemies of Christian order deserving death. The Carolingian legislation drew on Old Testament prohibitions against sorcerers and diviners, embedding magic prohibition in a framework of religious obligation. This provided an early model for later medieval and early modern legislation that would treat witchcraft as both crime and sin.
historiographical_note: Richard Kieckhefer and Valerie Flint have analyzed Carolingian magic legislation as part of the Christianization process, noting that it created a framework defining magic as diabolically inspired that differed from earlier Roman legal categories. However, historians note that enforcement was uneven and the legislation's practical impact on actual prosecutions remains debated.
source_method: MGH Capitularia Regum Francorum; secondary scholarship on Carolingian law and religion
